title.narrative: FAO SSD Improving resilient livelihoods, food and nutrition security 2021-2024
FAO SSD Improving resilient livelihoods, food and nutrition security 2021-2024

description.narrative:
Sida stödjer projektet "Improving resilient livelihoods through food and nutrition security of vulnerable communities, especially women-headed households in Wau and Torit States of South Sudan" under perioden 2021- 2024 med totalt 60 000 000 SEK.
Det övergripande syftet med projektet är att bidra till att bygga upp motståndskraften hos de mest utsatta hushållen, särskilt de som leds av kvinnor, i de mest livsmedelsosäkra regionerna i Sydsudan. Projektet förväntas bidra till att omkring 48 000 människor får möjlighet att utveckla metoder för ett mångsidigt och klimatanpassat jordbruk, liksom ökad kapacitet för ett hållbart nyttjande av naturresurser och land med fokus på sårbara hushåll, kvinnor, barn, återvändare och internfördrivna flyktingar.
Projektet avser att öka möjligheterna till en hållbar försörjning med fokus på diversifierad jordbruksproduktion, liksom att stärka livsmedels- och näringstrygghet för sårbara hushåll, så att de därmed inte behöver vidta negativa hanteringsåtgärder på grund av att de utsätts för externa risker orsakade av klimatförändringar och osäkerhet, bland annat åsamkat av konflikt. Projektet ska samtidigt bidra till att stärka lokal kapacitet att förebygga och hantera naturresursrelaterade konflikter, samt bidra till att stärka kvinnors ekonomiska egenmakt genom bland annat aktiviteter som bidrar till att stärka inkomstmöjligheter för kvinnor.
Projektet implementeras i Wau och Torit, tidigare delstater i Västra Bahr El Ghazal och östra Ekvatoria. Wau och Torit har valts ut inom ramen för PfRR (Partnership for Recovery and Resilience), där produktionskapaciteten har påverkats drastiskt på grund av konflikter. En annan anledning till att fokusera på dessa två områden är på grund av ett stort antal återvändare i båda områdena.
Projektet har tre förväntade resultat: 1. Stärkt livsmedelskonsumtion på hushållsnivå. 2. Förbättrad näringsstatus och inkomst hos kvinnor och barn. 3. Reducerad sårbarhet för konflikter relaterade till land och naturresurser.
Sektor: 31120 - Agricultural development, 43073 - Food safety and quality. Policy markers: Gender equality (1 - Significant objective), Democracy and Human Rights (1-Significant objective), Disaster Risk Reduction (1-Significant objective), Conflict prevention, peace and security (1 - Significant objective), Employment (2 - Principal objective), Aid to environment (1 - Significant objective).

Sida supports the project "Improving resilient livelihoods through food and nutrition security of vulnerable communities, especially women-headed households in Wau and Torit States of South Sudan" for the period 2021-2024 with a total of 60 000 000 SEK.
The overall aim of the project is to contribute to building the resilience of the most vulnerable households, especially those headed by women, in the most food insecure regions of South Sudan. To achieve this, the project will support at least 8000 vulnerable households (approx. 48 000 individuals) engaged in agricultural activities in areas where there are IPC classifications of phase 3 and phase 4 - Crisis and Emergency levels of food insecurity.
The project aims to contribute to sustainable livelihood opportunities and food security, focusing on diversified agriculture and methods, as well as strengthening nutritional status and income of women and children, internally displaced people, returnees and vulnerable communities. The project is also expected to contribute to local capacity to prevent and reduce vulnerability to conflict related natural resources and communities access to land, as well as to promote women's economic empowerment through income generating activities and livelihood opportunities.
The project is implemented in Wau and Torit, former states of Western Bahr El Ghazal State and Eastern Equatoria. Wau and Torit have been selected within the framework och PfRR (Partnership for Recovery and Resilience), where the production capacities have been drastically affected due to conflict. Another reason for focusing on these two areas is because of the high numbers of returnees in both areas.
The project has three expected outcomes: 1. Enhanced households level food consumption. 2. Improved nutritional status and income of women and children. 3. Vulnerability to conflict related to communal access to land and other natural resources reduced.
Sectors: 31120 - Agricultural development, 43073 - Food safety and quality. Policy markers: Gender equality (1 - Significant objective), Democracy and Human Rights (1-Significant objective), Disaster Risk Reduction (1-Significant objective), Conflict prevention, peace and security (1 - Significant objective), Employment (2 - Principal objective), Aid to environment (1 - Significant objective).

The overall objective of the intervention is to contribute to building the resilience of the most vulnerable households, especially those headed by women in the most food insecure regions of South Sudan. This will be done through activities aimed at increasing agricultural productive capacity and incomes of vulnerable households, resulting in increased food availability, improved food consumption and nutritional outcomes, and ultimately contributing to improved resilience (adaptive and absorptive capacities) and food security.
The following are the expected outputs and a short summary of the indicators: Output 1: Access to diversified agriculture production and post-harvest handling inputs and technologies increased (number of households supported with production and post-harvest handling inputs and technologies, percent of houeholds reporting improved access to inputs and technologies, extent of sufficiency of productive/post-harvest handling inputs in meeting households needs),
Output 2: Access to information, skills and inputs for nutrition and climate sensitive agricultural production improved (Number of children and households supported to engage in nutrition sensitive school gardening, types of skills adopted and transferred to household production and food preparation),
Output 3: Womens economic empowerment promoted through nutrition-sensitive value chains and income-generating enterprises (Number of women supported to engage in value chains and income generating activities, types of value chains and income generating activities engaged in by women, average income earned by year from the value chains and income generating activities engaged in by women),
Output 4: Capacity to manage natural resource-related conflicts at community-level strengthened (Methodology for comprehensive natural resource-based conflict management capacity needs assessment developed, contextualized for different administrative levels, tested and validated, number of households mobilized to participate in community-based natural resource management, percent of community stakeholders reporting they believe the enhanced natural resource-based conflict management mechanisms will be useful in addressing the issue).

In brief, target households demonstrated significant improvements in both their resilience and dietary diversity. The Resilience Capacity Index (RCI) rose from a baseline of 48 to 62, recording a 29 percent increase, indicating greater ability to withstand and recover from shocks. Likewise, the Average Household Dietary Diversity Score (HDDS) increased from 5.5 in Torit and 6.4 in Wau at baseline, to 8.5 in Torit and 7.1 in Wau at endline. These gains reflect the projects multifaceted approach, including the distribution of climate-adapted inputs, training in climate-smart agriculture (CSA), conservation agriculture (CA) and broader economic and social interventions.
The outputs are described as largely successful in the final narrative report, with a few exceptions such as activity 4.2.4 Based on lessons learned from the previous project, implement a gender responsive, community based mapping and documentation of tenure rights, including disputes, natural resources and livelihoods, due to being beyond the projects available resources as land registry was not developed at the state level. Nevertheless, almost all indicators for outcomes and outputs in the logframe reached their end target, many times well beyond. A few examples of many successful results include:
Output 1
Between 2022 and 2024, a variety of crop (green grams, maize and sorghum) and vegetable (amaranthus, collards, cowpeas, green pepper, Jews mallow, okra and onion) seeds, as well as tools (hoes, rakes and sickles), were distributed to 1 000 women across eight OTP centres in Torit, 35 Womens Economic Empowerment (WEE) groups (11 crop production, 13 agro-processing, 3 tuber production, and 8 vegetable production groups), totaling 1 050 women and 16 youth groups. Each group cultivated between 1.5 and 2 feddans of land.
In Wau, similar inputs were distributed to 1 100 women across ten outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP) centres, 86 WEE groups comprised of 27 vegetable production, 29 crop production and 30 agro-processing groups (consisting of 2 600 females) and 51 crop production youth groups and 6 vegetable production youth groups. Each group cultivated between 1 and 2.5 feddans of land. In 2024, sweet potato vines and cassava cuttings were distributed to 1 100 women at the 10 OTP centres in Wau, and 1 000 women at the eight OTP centres in Torit. The women and youth reported increased production of vegetables and crops (83 percent in Torit and 63 percent in Wau), most of which was consumed at the household level, contributing to both crop and dietary diversification (74 percent in Torit and 81 percent in Wau).
In 2022, a total of 1 939 households (including 1 776 women) in Torit, and 2 400 households (including 1 765 women) in Wau were trained in climate-smart agricultural practices. The training covered topics such as planting on ridges and in basins, mulching, using drought- or flood-tolerant crop varieties, integrated pest management (IPM), crop diversification and post-harvest practices. Refresher training sessions were conducted in 2023 and 2024.
Output 2
In 2022, vegetable demonstration gardens were established: 20 gardens in Wau (ten in UNICEF-funded OTP centres and ten in primary schools) and 18 gardens in Torit (seven in UNICEF OTP centres and 11 in schools, including nine primary and two secondary schools). The vegetable demonstration gardens provided practical training for women and school children on how to grow various types of vegetables, including cowpeas, eggplant, Jews mallow, okra and tomatoes. The training covered techniques such as line planting, raising nursery beds, transplanting from the seedbed to the garden, weeding, mulching and gap filling. Additionally, the school demonstration gardens offered valuable knowledge on agriculture and nutrition to students. The women and school children applied the skills they had gained to establish their household vegetable gardens. Other community members requested participants to share the knowledge and skills gained from the project in vegetable production. One unexpected result from the UNICEF-funded OTP centres was they decided to keep the demonstration gardens after the trainings were conducted. Women joined voluntarily to maintain the gardens and teaching other beneficiaries, leading to a significant amount of unintended beneficiaries and boosted the sustainability of the activity.
Over the three-year project period, 1 100 women, including pregnant and lactating women, women of reproductive age, and women with children under five (CU5) from the UNICEF 10 OTP centres in Wau, and 1 000 women from 8 OTP centres in Torit, received vegetable seeds (such as eggplant, okra, amaranthus, eggplant, Jews mallow, okra and tomatoes) and gardening tools (hoes, rakes and watering cans) for home vegetable cultivation. These women were able to cultivate 1 to 1.5 feddans of land, leading to an increase in vegetable production. The vegetables were consumed at the household level, improving diets, while the surplus was sold to provide a source of income.
In 2023, a total of 9 600 fruit tree seedlings were distributed in Wau, including 5 400 mango seedlings and 4 200 guava seedlings, across ten OTP centres, ten primary schools and target households. In Torit, 5 129 fruit tree seedlings (comprising of 2 347 mangoes, 2 483 guavas and 299 citrus) were distributed to 11 schools, eight OTP centres and target households. It was reported that 60 percent of the trees are still growing, and it is anticipated that they will yield fruit for the target communities in the future.
Output 3
In 2023, a total of 2 600 women in Wau were selected and organized into 86 WEE groups, each consisting of 30 members. Additionally, 1 700 youth (including 368 women) were selected and formed into 56 groups. Of these, 28 youth groups were led by female chairpersons with male deputies, while the remaining 28 youth groups were led by male chairpersons with female deputies. These groups participated in enterprises that they selected. In Torit in 2023, 1 050 women were selected and organized into 35 WEE groups, each made up of 30 members and led by women. There were also 16 youth groups, each consisting of 30 members of both genders, with male youth leaders. These groups engaged in enterprises that they chose to pursue.
In 2023, various tools and equipment were distributed to WEE and youth groups in Torit based on the enterprises they had selected. A total of 120 watering cans were given to eight WEE vegetable production groups and four youth groups, while 240 watering cans were provided to eight OTPs and 330 to 11 schools for vegetable production. Additionally, 15 solar-powered irrigation pumps were distributed to 15 vegetable production groups, including ten WEE and five youth groups. Additionally, 13 agro-processing WEE groups received 13 weighing scales and 13 groundnut paste processing machines. Furthermore, youth, WEE and nutrition groups, along with 11 school agriculture clubs, received 345 pairs of tarpaulins for drying cowpeas and green grams. Moreover, 16 sorghum threshers were distributed to 11 WEE and five youth crop production groups, and three weighing scales and three cassava processing machines were provided to three WEE tuber production groups.
In Wau, 174 donkey ploughs were distributed: 84 to youth groups and 90 to WEE groups. Additionally, 30 weighing scales and eight manual groundnut shellers were provided to 30 WEE agro-processing groups. One power tiller was given to 29 WEE groups and another to 51 youth crop production groups. Moreover, 54 sorghum threshers were distributed to 29 WEE and 25 youth crop production groups. This equipment helped the crop production groups save time on farming activities, while the manual groundnut shellers allowed WEE agro-processing groups to reduce the time spent shelling groundnuts manually. In Wau, 84 percent of women reported improved vegetable production, 39 percent reported improved agro-processing and 53 percent reported an increase in their income. Similarly, in Torit, 85 percent of women experienced increased vegetable production, 52 percent improved agro-processing, and 50 percent saw a rise in income.
Output 4
In 2022, 300 households in Wau (including 150 women) were organized into ten Natural Resource Management Committees (NRMCs) (of which seven were newly established and three were pre-existing)). Similarly, in Torit, 300 households (including 150 women) were organized into ten NRMCs (eight newly established and two pre-existing). Each NRMC comprised of 30 members, equally divided between 15 women and 15 men. The selection of committee members in both locations was based on their standing and influence within the community, including chiefs, youth leaders, women leaders and other community members. This gender-balanced composition ensured that womens voices were included and actively involved in decision-making processes related to NRM and conflict resolution in their communities.
The project developed a radio programme called Giza ta Mara, Haak ta Mara in Juba Arabic, which translates to Women Nutrition, Women's Rights in English. This programme provided valuable information on women's nutrition and land rights and was broadcast in Torit and Wau.
In 2023, three episodes focusing on women's land rights were produced and aired on Eye Radio as part of the Ziraa Tanna program in Juba Arabic, meaning Our Farm in English. The programme aired every Friday at 17.30. Topics discussed included the importance of land and women's rights to access land in South Sudan, with a focus on the legal framework surrounding land ownership and womens rights. The programme also highlighted constitutional articles and the Land Act, specifically addressing women's land rights.
In Torit, from June 2023 to April 2024, the project collaborated with Radio Emmanuel 89 FM through the Catholic Radio Network, producing seven episodes on women's land rights, reaching an estimated 600 000 listeners (450 000 directly and 150 000 indirectly). The programme was broadcasted in three languages (simple Arabic, Acholi and Otuho) every Wednesday at 19.10. Additionally, a live-to-tape session on women's land rights was facilitated by technical staff in Torit, recorded in Juba Arabic.
From May to September 2024, Voice of Hope Radio in Wau produced seven radio talk shows on women's land rights in Arabic, Balanda and Lou. These aired every Monday, Wednesday and Friday at 07:00, allowing for quick and immediate listener feedback. The programmes are estimated to have reached 950 000 listeners across Western Bahr el Ghazal State. These radio programmes played a significant role in disseminating knowledge and raising awareness about womens land rights among project participants and the broader community.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
